simple: the place on a server's main board where one processor chip sits; a "two-socket server" has two processors.
analogy: one town.
precise: a physical processor package with its cores, caches, memory controllers and links; SMBIOS describes each populated or empty socket with one processor information structure (type 4).
source: D1 of F5-28 (John L. Hennessy, David A. Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach" (guide registry 4.2): chapters on memory-hierarchy design and on multiprocessors with distributed shared memory and directory-based coherence.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a group of processors and the memory that is nearest to them.
analogy: a town with its own library.
precise: a set of processors, memory ranges (and possibly devices) that the firmware declares to be close to each other; ACPI calls it a proximity domain and numbers it in the SRAT; the OS turns proximity domains into its NUMA nodes. Not to be confused with a "node" in distributed systems (F5-08), which is a whole machine.
source: D2 of F5-28 (UEFI Forum, "Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI) Specification" (curriculum item 20): the System Resource Affinity Table (processor local APIC affinity, memory affinity, flags), the System Locality Distance Information Table (normalised value 10), and the Heterogeneous Memory Attribute Table.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the firmware table that says which processors and which memory belong to which NUMA node.
analogy: the town register: who lives where, which library holds which shelves.
precise: the ACPI System Resource Affinity Table (signature "SRAT"): after the common header, a list of affinity structures, among them processor local APIC affinity (APIC ID → proximity domain) and memory affinity (base, length → proximity domain, with an "enabled" flag).
source: D2 of F5-28 (UEFI Forum, "Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI) Specification" (curriculum item 20): the System Resource Affinity Table (processor local APIC affinity, memory affinity, flags), the System Locality Distance Information Table (normalised value 10), and the Heterogeneous Memory Attribute Table.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the firmware table that says how far apart the NUMA nodes are.
analogy: the travel-time signs on the roads between towns.
precise: the ACPI System Locality Information Table (signature "SLIT"): a count n of localities followed by an n × n matrix of one-byte relative distances, where the distance of a locality to itself is normalised to 10.
source: D2 of F5-28 (UEFI Forum, "Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI) Specification" (curriculum item 20): the System Resource Affinity Table (processor local APIC affinity, memory affinity, flags), the System Locality Distance Information Table (normalised value 10), and the Heterogeneous Memory Attribute Table.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the wires and protocol that join the processors so they can reach each other's memory and keep caches consistent.
analogy: the bridge between the towns.
precise: point-to-point links between sockets that carry remote memory requests, responses and cache-coherence traffic; their names and properties are vendor-specific and come from the vendor's documentation for a named processor (AH-21).
source: D1 of F5-28 (John L. Hennessy, David A. Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach" (guide registry 4.2): chapters on memory-hierarchy design and on multiprocessors with distributed shared memory and directory-based coherence.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a NUMA node that has processors but no memory of its own.
analogy: a town with houses but no library: every book comes over the bridge.
precise: a proximity domain to which the SRAT assigns processors but no enabled memory range; every memory access from its processors is remote.
source: D2 of F5-28 (UEFI Forum, "Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI) Specification" (curriculum item 20): the System Resource Affinity Table (processor local APIC affinity, memory affinity, flags), the System Locality Distance Information Table (normalised value 10), and the Heterogeneous Memory Attribute Table.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the server's own operating system talks to its own BMC, from inside the box.
analogy: Sofia calling Tariq from inside the cottage.
precise: access to the management controller from the host through a host-side interface (KCS, SSIF or BT for IPMI; a host interface for Redfish); it needs a running host and host software, unlike out-of-band management (defined in OS305), which uses the BMC's own network connection and works whatever the host's state.
source: D1 of F5-29 (The IPMI promoters (Intel, Hewlett-Packard, NEC, Dell), "Intelligent Platform Management Interface Specification v2.0" (guide registry 4.5): the KCS interface chapter (registers, status bits, control codes, transfer phases), IPMI messaging (netfn/LUN, completion codes), the App, Chassis and Storage command chapters, the SEL record format, sensors and thresholds, IPMI over LAN.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the simplest way for the host's processor to pass IPMI messages to the BMC: two I/O registers and a byte-by-byte handshake.
analogy: a hatch in the gatehouse wall with one tray in each direction and a flag that says "tray full".
precise: Keyboard Controller Style interface: a data register and a status/command register; status bits OBF (output buffer full) and IBF (input buffer full) and a two-bit state (idle, read, write, error); control codes start and end a write phase and request each byte of the read phase.
source: D1 of F5-29 (The IPMI promoters (Intel, Hewlett-Packard, NEC, Dell), "Intelligent Platform Management Interface Specification v2.0" (guide registry 4.5): the KCS interface chapter (registers, status bits, control codes, transfer phases), IPMI messaging (netfn/LUN, completion codes), the App, Chassis and Storage command chapters, the SEL record format, sensors and thresholds, IPMI over LAN.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the BMC's diary of unusual events: a fan stopped, a temperature crossed a limit, the power went off.
analogy: Tariq's notebook.
precise: a non-volatile log of fixed-size records kept by the BMC, each with a record ID, a record type, a time stamp from the BMC's clock and, for system events, the generator, sensor type, sensor number, event type and event data; read and written with Storage commands.
source: D1 of F5-29 (The IPMI promoters (Intel, Hewlett-Packard, NEC, Dell), "Intelligent Platform Management Interface Specification v2.0" (guide registry 4.5): the KCS interface chapter (registers, status bits, control codes, transfer phases), IPMI messaging (netfn/LUN, completion codes), the App, Chassis and Storage command chapters, the SEL record format, sensors and thresholds, IPMI over LAN.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the first byte of every IPMI answer: 0 means "done", anything else says what went wrong.
analogy: Tariq's "yes, done" or "I don't know that code".
precise: a one-byte status in every IPMI response; 0x00 is success, and the Linux UAPI header in the build container names, among others, 0xC1 "invalid command" and 0xFF "unspecified".
source: L1 of F5-29 (Linux UAPI header /usr/include/linux/ipmi_msgdefs.h from the build container's package linux-libc-dev 6.8.0-146.146 (tier 4: what the Linux IPMI stack defines).)

simple: the one address a Redfish client must know; everything else is found from there.
analogy: the first page of the form book, listing all other forms.
precise: the top resource of a Redfish service, whose links lead to the collections of systems, chassis, managers and services; clients discover resources by following links rather than by building paths themselves.
source: D2 of F5-29 (DMTF, "Redfish Specification" and the Redfish schemas (guide registry 4.5; the registry records that the DMTF page returned "403 Forbidden"): service root, resources, collections, links, actions, OEM extensions, sessions and security.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: free, open firmware for the little management computer in a server.
analogy: the gatehouse team and its rule book.
precise: an open-source Linux distribution for BMCs, hosted by the Linux Foundation, built with the Yocto Project's tools from layers (common code plus per-machine layers), in which management functions are separate services that communicate over D-Bus; it offers Redfish, IPMI and a web interface.
source: D1 of F5-30 (OpenBMC project (Linux Foundation), "OpenBMC documentation" (guide registry 4.5): architecture (services on D-Bus, object paths, sensor, fan-control, logging and interface services), configuration, building images, running in QEMU.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the chip that is the BMC: a processor with all the controllers a server's management needs, on one piece of silicon.
analogy: the gatehouse itself, with its desk, phone and switches.
precise: a system-on-chip with one or more Arm cores, a DRAM controller, flash (SPI) controllers, Ethernet MACs, several UARTs, many I2C buses, ADC, PWM and fan-tachometer blocks, GPIOs and a host-facing interface (LPC or eSPI, with KCS registers); the Aspeed AST2600 is one such chip and QEMU models it.
source: D2 of F5-30 (QEMU project, "QEMU System Emulation User's Guide", section on Aspeed boards (the Arm system emulator's board list): machines, modelled devices, boot options.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a message system that lets programs on one computer offer objects, call each other's methods and announce changes.
analogy: the notice board.
precise: an inter-process communication system with a bus daemon, in which services own well-known names and export objects at paths; objects implement named interfaces with methods, properties and signals; clients read properties and subscribe to signals such as "properties changed".
source: D3 of F5-30 (freedesktop.org, "D-Bus Specification": bus, names, object paths, interfaces, properties, signals.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a program that runs in the background and does one job for as long as the computer is on.
analogy: one team member on shift.
precise: a long-running process without a terminal, started and supervised by the init system (systemd in OpenBMC), restarted when it fails according to its unit's settings.
source: D1 of F5-30 (OpenBMC project (Linux Foundation), "OpenBMC documentation" (guide registry 4.5): architecture (services on D-Bus, object paths, sensor, fan-control, logging and interface services), configuration, building images, running in QEMU.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: when the fan controller cannot see a temperature it needs, it runs the fans fast to be safe.
analogy: Bo's rule: thermometer missing, assume the worst.
precise: a fan-control policy that, on missing, stale or invalid inputs, sets the fans to a configured safe output (in the model of this chapter, 100 %), trading noise, power and fan wear for thermal safety.
source: D1 of F5-30 (OpenBMC project (Linux Foundation), "OpenBMC documentation" (guide registry 4.5): architecture (services on D-Bus, object paths, sensor, fan-control, logging and interface services), configuration, building images, running in QEMU.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the same program works on many boards because a file tells it which sensors and fans exist.
analogy: the instruction sheet that names each thermometer.
precise: board-specific facts (sensor names, buses, addresses, scaling, thresholds, fan zones) kept in data files (OpenBMC uses JSON and YAML files, among others) read by generic daemons at start-up, so that a new board is mostly a new configuration.
source: D1 of F5-30 (OpenBMC project (Linux Foundation), "OpenBMC documentation" (guide registry 4.5): architecture (services on D-Bus, object paths, sensor, fan-control, logging and interface services), configuration, building images, running in QEMU.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: starting a computer from a file it fetches over the network instead of from its own disk.
analogy: Lina's starter parcel.
precise: a boot in which the firmware's boot manager selects a network boot option, obtains an address and a boot-file location from the network (DHCP), downloads the file (TFTP or HTTP) and executes it.
source: D1 of F5-31 (UEFI Forum, "Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) Specification" (curriculum item 19): boot manager and load options, device path protocol and node types, loaded image protocol, PXE base code protocol, HTTP boot, Secure Boot.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the long-established standard way for a computer's firmware to boot from the network.
analogy: the rule "shout 'I'm new here', then fetch the parcel from the depot".
precise: a specification, originally from Intel, that defines how a client's firmware uses DHCP (with PXE-specific options) to find a boot server and file, and TFTP to download it; UEFI firmware implements it as the PXE Base Code protocol for IPv4 and IPv6.
source: D2 of F5-31 (Intel Corporation, "Preboot Execution Environment (PXE) Specification" version 2.1: the PXE DHCP options and boot sequence.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a very simple file-download protocol, small enough to fit in firmware.
analogy: the depot that hands out parcels piece by piece, by exact name.
precise: the Trivial File Transfer Protocol over UDP: a read request names the file; the server sends numbered blocks, each acknowledged before the next; errors are sent as error packets with a code and a message; no authentication, no directory listing.
source: D3 of F5-31 (IETF, RFC 1350 "The TFTP Protocol (Revision 2)" and the TFTP option RFCs (2347, 2348, 2349); IETF, RFC 2131 "Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol" and RFC 4578 (DHCP options for PXE) (curriculum item 50).) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the first program a computer downloads and runs when it boots from the network.
analogy: the starter parcel.
precise: the file named by the DHCP boot-file option and downloaded by the PXE client; on UEFI it is a UEFI application (in the lab, BOOTX64.EFI built from netboot.cc); in practice it is often a boot loader that fetches a kernel or an installer.
source: D2 of F5-31 (Intel Corporation, "Preboot Execution Environment (PXE) Specification" version 2.1: the PXE DHCP options and boot sequence.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: network boot that downloads the boot file with the web's protocol instead of TFTP.
analogy: a courier with a van instead of carrying the parcel in pieces.
precise: a UEFI network boot method in which DHCP returns a URI and the firmware downloads the image over HTTP (or HTTPS), which is faster over long distances and can cross routers more easily than TFTP.
source: D1 of F5-31 (UEFI Forum, "Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) Specification" (curriculum item 19): boot manager and load options, device path protocol and node types, loaded image protocol, PXE base code protocol, HTTP boot, Secure Boot.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a description, step by step, of where a device sits, like "root, then PCI slot 2, then the network card with this MAC".
analogy: directions to the depot: town, street, building.
precise: a sequence of variable-length nodes (type, subtype, 16-bit length, data) ending with an end node of type 0x7f, attached to a handle through the device path protocol; boot options and loaded images refer to devices with it.
source: D1 of F5-31 (UEFI Forum, "Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) Specification" (curriculum item 19): boot manager and load options, device path protocol and node types, loaded image protocol, PXE base code protocol, HTTP boot, Secure Boot.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the list of what a server is and has: maker, serial number, processors, memory.
analogy: the moving company's checklist.
precise: machine-readable facts used to identify and plan servers, here read from SMBIOS structures 0 (firmware), 1 (system, with serial number and UUID), 3 (chassis, asset tag), 4 (processor sockets) and 17 (memory devices), and checked against an independent record.
source: D4 of F5-31 (DMTF, "System Management BIOS (SMBIOS) Reference Specification" (curriculum item 21): types 0, 1 (including the UUID encoding), 3, 4 and 17.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a processor that a VM sees, which is really a share of a real processor.
analogy: a bed in a flat, which may share a room with others when the guesthouse is full.
precise: a virtual processor of a guest, in KVM-based hypervisors implemented as a thread of the VM's process that the host scheduler runs on a physical CPU (pCPU) and that enters guest mode to execute guest instructions.
source: D1 of F5-32 (QEMU project, "QEMU System Emulation User's Guide" (accelerators KVM and TCG, CPU models and features, migration) and the Linux kernel documentation, "The Definitive KVM API Documentation".) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: promising VMs more processors or memory in total than the host really has, betting they will not all use it at once.
analogy: renting more beds than rooms.
precise: allocating virtual resources beyond the physical ones, expressed as a ratio (for example vCPUs per pCPU); CPU overcommit costs waiting time (steal time) when guests are busy together; memory overcommit needs reclaiming mechanisms (ballooning, page sharing, swapping) and risks severe slowdowns or failures when guests use what they were promised.
source: D2 of F5-32 (James E. Smith, Ravi Nair, "Virtual Machines: Versatile Platforms for Systems and Processes" (Morgan Kaufmann): system virtual machines, resource virtualization, binary translation.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: QEMU's way of running a guest without hardware help: it translates the guest's instructions into the host's instructions in software.
analogy: a tenant whose every instruction is read aloud by an interpreter.
precise: QEMU's dynamic binary translator: guest code is translated block by block into host code and cached; it works on any host and for other architectures, but is slower than hardware-assisted virtualization, by an amount that depends strongly on the kind of instructions (R4, R5).
source: D1 of F5-32 (QEMU project, "QEMU System Emulation User's Guide" (accelerators KVM and TCG, CPU models and features, migration) and the Linux kernel documentation, "The Definitive KVM API Documentation".) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: moving a running VM to another host without switching it off.
analogy: moving a tenant to another guesthouse while she sleeps, so she wakes up in the same-looking flat.
precise: transferring a VM's memory, device state and vCPU state to another host while it runs: commonly pre-copy, which copies memory in rounds while the guest keeps writing, tracks dirtied pages, then pauses the guest briefly to copy the rest and resumes it on the destination.
source: D4 of F5-32 (Christopher Clark et al., "Live Migration of Virtual Machines" (NSDI 2005): pre-copy migration.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: giving a VM a real device (a network card, a GPU) for itself instead of an imitation.
analogy: a flat with its own private entrance and its own boiler.
precise: assigning a physical PCI device or a virtual function of an SR-IOV device to a guest, with the IOMMU translating and confining the device's DMA to the guest's memory; fast and isolated, but it ties the VM to the host's hardware and complicates live migration.
source: D2 of F5-32 (James E. Smith, Ravi Nair, "Virtual Machines: Versatile Platforms for Systems and Processes" (Morgan Kaufmann): system virtual machines, resource virtualization, binary translation.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: another VM on the same host that slows yours down by using shared parts heavily.
analogy: the tenant who takes hour-long showers.
precise: interference between co-located guests through resources the hypervisor does not partition fully: CPU time under overcommit, last-level cache, memory bandwidth, the inter-socket link, network and storage queues.
source: D3 of F5-32 (Luiz André Barroso, Urs Hölzle, Parthasarathy Ranganathan, "The Datacenter as a Computer: Designing Warehouse-Scale Machines" (Synthesis Lectures on Computer Architecture): consolidation, resource sharing, interference.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the box in a server that turns mains electricity into the low voltages the electronics use.
analogy: the water meter and pressure reducer where the house joins the mains.
precise: a converter from AC (or high-voltage DC) input to the server's main DC rail(s), often hot-swappable and duplicated; it reports input and output power, temperatures and faults to the BMC over a management bus (PMBus on SMBus/I2C).
source: D2 of F5-33 (The server vendor's hardware and maintenance documentation for the platform used in a real lab, and the PMBus Specification (SMIF / System Management Interface Forum): PSUs, fans, sensors, hot-swap procedures, power capping.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the temperature of the air entering the front of the server.
analogy: how warm the street air is when it comes through the bakery's wall fans.
precise: the temperature at the server's air intake, measured by a front-panel sensor; it is the starting point of every temperature inside, so a warmer inlet raises every component's temperature for the same power and airflow; data-centre operators set it through the room's cooling.
source: D3 of F5-33 (Luiz André Barroso, Urs Hölzle, Parthasarathy Ranganathan, "The Datacenter as a Computer: Designing Warehouse-Scale Machines": power delivery, cooling, failures and repairs.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the server switches itself off because it is too hot, to avoid damage.
analogy: the bakery alarm that switches the ovens off.
precise: a protective power-off triggered by firmware (the BMC on an upper-critical threshold, or the OS on an ACPI critical trip point) or by the processor's own hardware trip at its maximum temperature, after the softer measures (fans, throttling) were not enough.
source: D1 of F5-33 (The IPMI promoters (Intel, Hewlett-Packard, NEC, Dell), "Intelligent Platform Management Interface Specification v2.0" (guide registry 4.5): sensor types, thresholds, SEL event formats, chassis power restore policy.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the rule for whether a server switches itself back on after its power went away.
analogy: "switch the ovens back on when the power returns".
precise: a BMC or firmware setting with values such as always off, always on, or restore the previous state; it decides what happens after an AC loss or, on some platforms, after a protective shutdown; "always on" can turn a protective shutdown into a cycle.
source: D1 of F5-33 (The IPMI promoters (Intel, Hewlett-Packard, NEC, Dell), "Intelligent Platform Management Interface Specification v2.0" (guide registry 4.5): sensor types, thresholds, SEL event formats, chassis power restore policy.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long a part works on average before it fails, and how long it takes on average to fix it.
analogy: how often a pipe bursts, and how long the plumber takes to come.
precise: mean time between failures and mean time to repair (restore); with constant failure rates, the steady-state availability of a repairable part is MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). An MTBF is a statistical rate over a population, not a lifetime of one part.
source: D6 of F5-33 (A reliability-engineering textbook chosen by the Source Researcher (for example Patrick D. T. O'Connor, Andre Kleyner, "Practical Reliability Engineering"): MTBF, MTTR, availability, k-of-n systems.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one more part than needed, so that one can fail without harm.
analogy: a second water pipe from another street.
precise: a configuration with N + 1 identical parts where N suffice (for example 1+1 power supplies, 3+1 fans); the system survives any single failure, provided the failure is detected and repaired before a second one, and provided the remaining parts can carry the load in all conditions.
source: D6 of F5-33 (A reliability-engineering textbook chosen by the Source Researcher (for example Patrick D. T. O'Connor, Andre Kleyner, "Practical Reliability Engineering"): MTBF, MTTR, availability, k-of-n systems.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
